newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan Oct customs-cleared trade data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan Oct customs-cleared trade data.

text.p: The following is a selection of analysts' reactions to Japan's customs-cleared trade data for October released Monday, which showed a year-on-year drop of 12.9 percent to 470.86 billion yen.
"It (the figure) was slightly surprising after the surplus in the first 20 days of October showed a rise of more than 20 percent... The decline in the trade surplus is decelerating."
JESPER KOLL, CHIEF ECONOMIST, JP MORGAN:

"What you see here is that the rise in the trade surplus with the U.S. is almost entirely due to the cutback of reverse imports. Japanese carmakers are now substituting U.S. products with Japanese products to meet Japanese demand. That is really the driving force here."

"This (the overall trade surplus decline) is a fortunate number for Japan in the short term, but longer term what we are seeing in the U.S.-Japan trade balance is signalling a rise in the global surplus down the road."

"Automobile exports to the United States are certain to continue a year-on-year increase, but at the same time, auto exports were hit hard by the strong yen 12 months ago, and part of the reason we see the strong increase (in exports to the United States) is because it was extremely weak 12 months ago.
"But as the overall export prices of Japanese products have been decreasing, we will see a reasonable year-on-year increase.
"As for market impact, as the surplus dropped, I see only a little impact on the markets.
MASARU TAKAGI, CHIEF ECONOMIST, FUJI RESEARCH INSTITUTE:

"Almost two years have passed since we began seeing a decline of customs-cleared trade figures, but today, the situation is completely changed. It's almost a flat situation, or a little bit of a downward situation compared with a year earlier.
"There is the structural change of trade, that is the shift of production from Japan to overseas, where we see a huge inflow of foreign goods from Asian countries and the United States continuing.

"The structural trend (of a declining trade surplus) is continuing. But at the same time, the foreign-exchange effect, that is the cheaper yen, will have an effect on Japanese exports. So in the near future, we will see a so-called "bottoming-out" phenomenon of the trade surplus.

"This new situation of the trade figures will start a stronger Japanese yen in the near future. My prediction is that the Japanese yen will be going between 103 and 113 yen against the U.S. dollar until the end of the next fiscal year.
